meta.blurb: A monk spent about eight years in a garden counting peas, and the numbers kept landing near three to one. Gregor Mendel's own paper shows how he found a hidden rule of inheritance, and how it lay forgotten until 1900.
meta.bible: Gregor Mendel: an Augustinian monk and teacher in the town of Brünn (now Brno, in the Czech Republic); patient, careful and modest; he read his paper in 1865 and it was printed in 1866; abbot from 1868; died 1884. The Natural History Society of Brünn: the audience for his two lectures. Pisum: the garden pea, his main plant. Phaseolus: the bean plants he also crossed. Hieracium: hawkweed, which behaved differently. Kölreuter and Gärtner: earlier breeders of hybrids; Carl Nägeli: the botanist who answered his letters. Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak: the three scientists who found his paper again in 1900. Key terms: Hybrid, Generation, Dominant, Recessive, Pollen, Anthers, Pistil, Ratio, Genes, Gene, Chromosomes, DNA, Genetics, Segregation, Independent Assortment, Abbot, Monastery. Facts: seven pairs of features (seed shape round or wrinkled; seed colour yellow or green; seed coat grey-brown or white; pod shape full or pinched; unripe pod colour green or yellow; flowers along the stem or at its tip; plant height tall or short); 34 kinds of pea tested, 22 kept; about eight years of experiments; second generation counts 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled, 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green, 787 tall to 277 short; two features together: 556 seeds in four groups of 315, 101, 108 and 32, close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; the word gene came long after Mendel. Voice and tone: clear, patient and warm, a scientist's paper told step by step; the numbers are real; where he was uncertain, the text says so. Added names and terms: Wrinkled (seed shape), Tweezers; Johann (Mendel's first name); Heinzendorf (now Hynčice) in Silesia, his birthplace, 1822; Theresia, his younger sister; Troppau (Opava) and Olomouc, where he studied; Cyril Napp, abbot until 1867; Christian Doppler and Franz Unger, his teachers in Vienna, 1851 to 1853; Thomas Knight and John Goss, English pea growers; Joseph Kölreuter, Carl Gärtner; Natural History Society of Brünn, founded about 1861; the two lectures on 8 February and 8 March 1865; Carl Nägeli of Munich, who received the paper in 1866 and advised him to try Hieracium; Mendel's second paper on Hieracium, 1869; abbot from 1868; the whirlwind of 1870; the monastery tax dispute from 1874; he died on 6 January 1884, aged 61. Rediscovery in 1900: Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak; William Bateson, who translated the paper in 1901 and named Genetics; Reginald Punnett (Punnett square, early twentieth century); Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri (chromosomes, 1902 to 1903); Wilhelm Johannsen (Gene, 1909); Thomas Hunt Morgan (fruit flies, from 1910; Linkage); Archibald Garrod (1902); James Watson, Francis Crick and Rosalind Franklin (DNA, 1953); Ronald Fisher (1936); Mirabilis, the marvel of Peru; Starch; Genome. Letters: A and a for the dominant and recessive forms of seed shape, B and b for seed colour; AaBb is the double hybrid. Further facts: second generation counts of the other features: 705 purple-red to 224 white flowers, 882 full to 299 pinched pods, 428 green to 152 yellow unripe pods, 651 to 207 flowers along the stem to flowers at the top; third generation: of 565 round-seeded plants 193 bred true and 372 did not, of 519 yellow-seeded plants 166 and 353; back-cross counts 31, 26, 27, 26 and 24, 25, 22, 26; of 301 round yellow seeds sown, 38, 65, 60 and 138 plants of four kinds; with n pairs of features a hybrid makes 2 to the power n kinds of cells and 3 to the power n kinds of plant.

beats.scene: Mendel walks between rows of pea plants in a quiet monastery garden
beats.summary: Gregor Mendel, a monk in the town of Brünn, begins a long series of careful plant experiments.

beats.scene: A boy helps his father graft young fruit trees on a small farm
beats.summary: Johann Mendel is born in 1822 into a farming family in Silesia and grows up working with plants and trees.

beats.scene: A village teacher shows a clever farm boy a book in a small school
beats.summary: A teacher sees that Johann learns unusually fast and sends him to a better school in the town of Troppau.

beats.scene: A young woman hands a small purse of savings to her brother
beats.summary: When the family's money runs short, his younger sister Theresia gives up part of her savings so that he can keep studying.

beats.scene: A student writes by candlelight in a small room full of books
beats.summary: Mendel studies philosophy, mathematics and physics at Olomouc, but money is still short and worry sometimes makes him ill.

beats.scene: A young man in a plain robe enters a large old monastery gate
beats.summary: In 1843 he joins the Augustinian monastery in Brünn and takes the name Gregor.

beats.scene: Monks study rocks, plants and old books in a large monastery library
beats.summary: The abbot, Cyril Napp, welcomes science, and the monastery has a library, collections of plants and minerals, and a garden.

beats.scene: A young monk teaches a classroom of attentive boys
beats.summary: Mendel teaches as a substitute teacher and is liked by his pupils, but in 1850 he fails the examination that would make him a full teacher.

beats.scene: A lecture hall in Vienna with a professor, a chalkboard and rows of students
beats.summary: From 1851 to 1853 Mendel studies at the University of Vienna, learning physics from Christian Doppler and the science of plants from Franz Unger.

beats.scene: Mendel stands at a window looking over the monastery garden, a notebook in hand
beats.summary: Back in Brünn in 1853 he teaches at the local school and begins to wonder how plants pass their features on to their young.

beats.scene: A farmer shows a young calf that looks just like its mother
beats.summary: People have always seen that young animals and plants look like their parents, and farmers have chosen the best parents for thousands of years.

beats.scene: Sheep farmers in Moravia compare the wool of two different sheep
beats.summary: Around Brünn, farmers and fruit growers argue about how to improve sheep, wool and fruit by choosing parents.

beats.scene: Two jars of paint, red and white, are mixed into pink
beats.summary: Many people believed that the features of two parents simply blend in their young, like paints mixed together.

beats.scene: A gardener holds a red flower and a white flower together
beats.summary: A cross between two different kinds of plant gives a hybrid, and gardeners made hybrids to get new colours and shapes.

beats.scene: An old botanist examines tobacco flowers through a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Around 1760 Joseph Kölreuter makes hybrids of tobacco plants with great care and shows that both parents have a share in the young plant.

beats.scene: Two crosses are drawn side by side with the parents' roles reversed
beats.summary: Kölreuter finds that it makes no difference which parent gives the pollen, because the hybrid is the same either way.

beats.scene: A German gardener fills thick notebooks with hundreds of plant names
beats.summary: Carl Gärtner makes many thousands of crosses on hundreds of kinds of plant over many years, but finds no simple law.

beats.scene: Two English gardeners compare pods of peas, one grey and one white
beats.summary: Growers such as Thomas Knight and John Goss had crossed peas earlier and had noticed that a feature could vanish and then return.

beats.scene: Mendel sits at a desk with books and a notebook, comparing old results
beats.summary: Mendel reads all of this and sees what is missing: nobody has followed single features through the generations and counted every plant.

beats.scene: Mendel writes a heading about the law of hybrids across a notebook page
beats.summary: Mendel decides to look for the law by which hybrids form, knowing that it will take years of patient work on very many plants.

beats.scene: Mendel lists three needs for an experimental plant on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: A good plant for the work must pass three tests: clear lasting differences, flowers that keep out foreign pollen, and fertile hybrids.

beats.scene: Two pea plants of different heights grow side by side with labels
beats.summary: First, the plant must have clear differences between its varieties, and they must be passed on unchanged generation after generation.

beats.scene: A bee hovers near a flower while another flower is wrapped in cloth
beats.summary: Second, the flowers of the hybrids must be protected from stray pollen from other plants, or the experiment would be spoiled.

beats.scene: A grown hybrid plant is covered in pods full of seeds
beats.summary: Third, the hybrids and their young must be fertile, so that the experiment can go on through many generations.

beats.scene: A cut-away drawing of a pea flower shows the keel and its parts
beats.summary: The pea belongs to the legume family, and its flower has a boat-shaped keel that wraps the pollen-bearing parts and the pistil.

beats.scene: Pollen falls from the anthers onto the pistil inside a closed pea flower
beats.summary: The pollen is shed inside the closed flower, often before the bud opens, so the pea normally fertilises itself.

beats.scene: Rows of pea plants of the same variety stand pure and even
beats.summary: Because of this, pea varieties stay pure for generations, and any surprise in the young plants must come from Mendel's own crosses.

beats.scene: Packets of pea seeds from many seed merchants are laid out on a table
beats.summary: Mendel gets 34 varieties of pea from seed dealers and sows them to see which ones are really constant.

beats.scene: Mendel compares plants from year to year in a notebook, crossing some out
beats.summary: He tests the varieties for two years and keeps the 22 that always breed true, setting aside the ones that vary.

beats.scene: Mendel ties tall pea plants to stakes while a beetle crawls on a pod
beats.summary: He grows the peas in garden beds with sticks to hold them up, and he guards against the pea beetle, which can ruin seeds.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass is held over two peas that look slightly different
beats.summary: Mendel decides to use only features that are sharp and clear, not ones that differ by 'more or less'.

beats.scene: A round pea and a wrinkled pea sit side by side on a palm
beats.summary: The first pair is the shape of the ripe seed: round, or angular and deeply wrinkled.

beats.scene: Yellow peas and green peas lie in two small piles on a plate
beats.summary: The second pair is the colour of the seed itself, yellow or green, seen through the thin seed coat.

beats.scene: A grey-brown seed coat and a white seed coat beside purple and white flowers
beats.summary: The third pair is the colour of the seed coat, which goes with the flower: grey-brown seeds come with purple-red flowers, white seeds with white flowers.

beats.scene: A plump smooth pod lies beside a pod pinched between the seeds
beats.summary: The fourth pair is the shape of the ripe pod: smooth and full, or pinched in between the seeds.

beats.scene: A green pod and a bright yellow pod hang on neighbouring plants
beats.summary: The fifth pair is the colour of the unripe pod: green or yellow.

beats.scene: Flowers grow along the stem on one plant and at the tip on another
beats.summary: The sixth pair is where the flowers sit: along the stem, or bunched at the top.

beats.scene: A very tall pea plant stands beside a short one with a measuring stick
beats.summary: The seventh pair is the length of the stem: tall plants of about six or seven feet, or short ones of under two feet.

beats.scene: Seven small cards are laid in a row, each showing two forms
beats.summary: Altogether Mendel has seven pairs of features, and every plant shows one form or the other in each pair.

beats.scene: Rows of numbered pea plots stretch across a sunlit monastery garden
beats.summary: The experiments last about eight years and use many thousands of plants, all counted one by one.

beats.scene: A tray holds fine tweezers, a small brush, string and paper bags
beats.summary: To make a cross, Mendel needs only a few small tools: fine tweezers, a soft brush, bags and labels.

beats.scene: Mendel gently presses open the keel of a young pea flower
beats.summary: He chooses a young flower whose bud is still closed and gently opens the keel to reach the parts inside.

beats.scene: Mendel opens a pea bud with tweezers and removes its small yellow anthers
beats.summary: Before the pollen ripens, he removes the anthers with the tweezers so that the flower cannot fertilise itself.

beats.scene: A brush carries yellow pollen from one flower to another flower
beats.summary: He takes pollen from the chosen father plant and dusts it onto the sticky tip of the pistil of the prepared flower.

beats.scene: A small paper bag is tied gently over a pea flower
beats.summary: He covers the flower with a small bag so that insects and the wind cannot bring any other pollen.

beats.scene: Labelled tags hang on pea plants, each with a small number
beats.summary: Each crossed flower gets a label, so that Mendel can always tell which parents made which pods.

beats.scene: Two plants swap roles, each in turn giving pollen to the other
beats.summary: He makes each cross both ways, using each kind of plant once as the pollen parent and once as the seed parent.

beats.scene: Pods ripen on a plant while others hang on a plant left alone
beats.summary: To raise the next generation he leaves the hybrid plants alone to fertilise themselves in their natural way.

beats.scene: Mendel works in the early light among pea flowers in late spring
beats.summary: The work must be done in a few weeks in spring, when the flowers are in bloom, and every flower needs attention at the right moment.

beats.scene: Dry pea pods are opened and seeds are counted into small paper packets
beats.summary: In summer and autumn the pods ripen, and Mendel opens each one, counts the seeds, sorts them by form and stores them in labelled packets.

beats.scene: Mendel holds a round pea in one hand, a wrinkled one in the other
beats.summary: The first cross joins plants with round seeds to plants with wrinkled seeds, and Mendel waits to see what the young plants will make.

beats.scene: A pod opens to show only smooth round seeds in a neat row
beats.summary: When the pods are opened, every seed is round: the wrinkled form has disappeared from the first generation.

beats.scene: Yellow seeds fill a pod from a cross, with no green seed among them
beats.summary: The same happens with colour: when yellow-seeded plants are crossed with green-seeded ones, every seed is yellow.

beats.scene: Seven pairs of features are listed with one form in each circled
beats.summary: Mendel does the same with each of the other pairs, and in every case the first generation looks like only one of the two parents.

beats.scene: A table lists seven winning forms beside seven faded ones
beats.summary: The winners are round seeds, yellow seeds, grey-brown coats, full pods, green pods, flowers along the stem and tall plants.

beats.scene: A drawing shows a large bold letter above a smaller faded one
beats.summary: Mendel names the feature that passes into the hybrid unchanged dominant, because it dominates its partner.

beats.scene: A faded outline of a seed sits behind a bold one
beats.summary: The feature that seems to vanish he calls recessive, because it seems to step back and hide.

beats.scene: Two arrows between plants point both ways, and the results look the same
beats.summary: Whether the dominant form came with the pollen or with the egg cell made no difference to the result.

beats.scene: A hybrid pea plant looks just like its dominant parent standing beside it
beats.summary: In peas the hybrid looks like one parent and not like a blend, which is unlike the intermediate hybrids of many other plants.

beats.scene: A tall healthy pea plant stands in the sun with a question mark above
beats.summary: The first generation looks simple, but Mendel asks what has become of the hidden form and plans to find out.

beats.scene: Hybrid seeds are pushed into spring soil in tidy rows
beats.summary: The next spring Mendel sows the hybrid seeds and lets the plants fertilise themselves, to raise a second generation.

beats.scene: The pods of a hybrid plant hold both round and wrinkled seeds
beats.summary: In the second generation the wrinkled seeds are back, so the hidden form had been waiting and had not been destroyed.

beats.scene: A neat table lists seeds in two columns, round and wrinkled
beats.summary: He counts them: of 7,324 seeds from the hybrids, 5,474 are round and 1,850 are wrinkled, about three to one.

beats.scene: Yellow and green seeds are counted into two dishes
beats.summary: For seed colour, 6,022 seeds are yellow and 2,001 are green: again about three to one.

beats.scene: Purple-red and white pea flowers bloom on neighbouring plants
beats.summary: For seed coat and flower colour, 705 plants have purple-red flowers and 224 have white flowers.

beats.scene: A plump pod and a pinched pod are laid out in two rows
beats.summary: For pod shape, 882 plants have full pods and 299 have pinched ones.

beats.scene: Green and yellow unripe pods hang side by side on the stems
beats.summary: For the colour of the unripe pod, 428 plants have green pods and 152 have yellow pods.

beats.scene: Flowers grow along the stems on some plants and at the tops on others
beats.summary: For the position of the flowers, 651 plants have flowers along the stem and 207 have them at the top.

beats.scene: A table of seven pairs of features with their counts beside them
beats.summary: For the length of the stem, 787 plants are tall and 277 are short.

beats.scene: A wall chart lists all seven ratios in a single column
beats.summary: Altogether Mendel counted close to 20,000 seeds and plants in this generation, and in every pair the dominant form outnumbered the other by about three to one.

beats.scene: A table shows counts close to three to one but never exact
beats.summary: The numbers are close to three to one but never exact, and Mendel does not hide the small differences.

beats.scene: A man tosses a coin many times and writes down each result
beats.summary: Chance explains the differences, as with a coin: a few tosses give uneven results, but thousands of tosses come close to half heads.

beats.scene: Small piles of seeds from single pods show very uneven ratios
beats.summary: In single pods and single plants the ratios swing widely, which shows why a small experiment could mislead.

beats.scene: Mendel adds columns of figures at a desk piled with notebooks
beats.summary: So Mendel adds up the counts from all the plants, and the real ratio appears out of the crowd.

beats.scene: Two seeds lie on a table, one beside a seedling, one beside a flower
beats.summary: Features of the seed show in the seeds themselves, while features of the plant show only after sowing, so some results come a year sooner.

beats.scene: A single hybrid plant stands alone in its own labelled row
beats.summary: The next question: if the hidden form comes back, is it the same as before, or changed by its time in hiding?

beats.scene: Seeds from each second-generation plant are sown in their own labelled row
beats.summary: In the third generation, Mendel sows the seeds of every second-generation plant in a separate row, to follow each family.

beats.scene: Rows of plants grown from wrinkled seeds all bear wrinkled seeds
beats.summary: Plants from the wrinkled seeds, the recessive form, always breed true: all their offspring are wrinkled for as long as he follows them.

beats.scene: Rows of plants grown from green seeds all bear green seeds
beats.summary: The same is true for green seeds and the other recessive forms: they all breed true.

beats.scene: Mendel looks at rows of round-seeded plants and wonders about two different groups
beats.summary: The plants with the dominant form are different: they do not all breed alike, and they need a closer look.

beats.scene: Mendel marks many round-seeded plants with numbers in a notebook
beats.summary: He chooses more than five hundred plants with the dominant form for each of two features, and sows seeds from each one.

beats.scene: A row of plants all with round seeds sits beside a mixed row
beats.summary: Some plants give only the dominant form and so are pure; others give both forms again, in three to one, and so are hybrids.

beats.scene: Tally marks in a notebook: few pure plants, many mixed ones
beats.summary: For seed shape, of 565 plants, 193 give only round seeds and 372 give both forms: about one to two.

beats.scene: A second notebook page shows the same counting for yellow seeds
beats.summary: For seed colour, of 519 plants, 166 give only yellow seeds and 353 give both: again about one to two.

beats.scene: The mixed plants produce round and wrinkled seeds in a three-to-one share
beats.summary: The mixed plants, grown on, give three to one again, just as the first hybrids did.

beats.scene: A diagram splits a family tree into one quarter, two quarters and one quarter
beats.summary: So the three-to-one ratio hides one to two to one: one quarter pure dominant, one half hybrid and one quarter pure recessive.

beats.scene: Mendel marks a quarter, a half and a quarter on each of seven columns
beats.summary: He checks all seven pairs of features, and the one-two-one pattern holds in each of them.

beats.scene: Two peas that look the same, one pure and one carrying a hidden form
beats.summary: A plant that shows the dominant form can be pure or a hybrid, and only its offspring show which.

beats.scene: A grid shows a hybrid's offspring splitting again in every new generation
beats.summary: Each generation of self-fertilised hybrids splits again, with half of the offspring hybrids once more, so the share of hybrids keeps shrinking.

beats.scene: A bar chart shows the hybrids shrinking by half in each generation
beats.summary: After ten generations, among 2,048 plants, 1,023 would be pure dominant, 1,023 pure recessive and only two hybrids.

beats.scene: Letters on a page: a large A, a small a, and pairs of them
beats.summary: Mendel uses letters to show the pattern: A for the dominant form, a for the recessive form, and Aa for the hybrid.

beats.scene: A line of letters reads A plus two Aa plus a
beats.summary: The second generation is written A + 2Aa + a: one pure dominant, two hybrids and one pure recessive.

beats.scene: Mendel draws two kinds of small dots for pollen and two for egg cells
beats.summary: Mendel's idea: a hybrid makes two kinds of pollen cells and two kinds of egg cells, in equal numbers, and each cell carries only one form.

beats.scene: A pure plant makes only one kind of pollen, shown as identical dots
beats.summary: A pure plant makes only one kind of cell, because it carries the same form on both sides.

beats.scene: Two bags of marbles are drawn at random, one marble from each
beats.summary: Which pollen meets which egg cell is a matter of chance, like drawing one marble from each of two bags.

beats.scene: Four small boxes show every pairing of two kinds of pollen and egg cells
beats.summary: There are four possible pairings: A with A, A with a, a with A, and a with a, each equally likely.

beats.scene: Three of four boxes show the dominant form, one shows the hidden form
beats.summary: Three of the four pairings show the dominant form and one shows the recessive form, which explains three to one.

beats.scene: Boxes labelled one, two and one show pure, hybrid and pure plants
beats.summary: The same pairings explain one to two to one: A with A is pure dominant, the two mixed pairings are hybrids, and a with a is pure recessive.

beats.scene: Mendel's hand draws a line separating two kinds of cells inside a pea flower
beats.summary: The key point is that the two forms in a hybrid do not blend or damage one another; they stay separate and are sorted again into different cells.

beats.scene: Mendel looks at a tiny pollen grain through a simple microscope
beats.summary: Mendel never sees any of this happening inside the cells; he reasons from the numbers alone.

beats.scene: Mendel writes the word prediction above two columns in his notebook
beats.summary: A good explanation must also predict something new, so Mendel looks for a test that could prove his idea wrong.

beats.scene: A hybrid plant is crossed back with a plant of the hidden kind
beats.summary: Test one: cross a hybrid with the pure recessive plant. His theory predicts equal numbers of hybrids and pure recessive plants.

beats.scene: A hybrid plant is crossed with a pure plant of the dominant kind
beats.summary: Test two: cross a hybrid with the pure dominant plant. The prediction is that every young plant shows the dominant form, though half of them are hybrids.

beats.scene: Two flowers are crossed, with four different pea seeds lying around them
beats.summary: To make the test sharper, Mendel uses two features at once, so that his theory predicts four equal groups instead of two.

beats.scene: A hybrid with round yellow seeds receives pollen from a wrinkled green plant
beats.summary: He fertilises hybrid flowers (round and yellow) with pollen of the wrinkled green plant and sorts the resulting seeds.

beats.scene: Four equal heaps of seeds: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green
beats.summary: The result: 31 round yellow, 26 round green, 27 wrinkled yellow and 26 wrinkled green, four groups of nearly equal size.

beats.scene: The cross is reversed: hybrid pollen is brushed onto a wrinkled green plant
beats.summary: He then reverses the cross, and the numbers are again nearly equal: 24, 25, 22 and 26.

beats.scene: Pollen cells and egg cells are shown as matching sets of four dots
beats.summary: So the hybrid makes all four kinds of cells in equal numbers, both as pollen and as egg cells.

beats.scene: Pods from a cross hold only seeds that all show the dominant forms
beats.summary: With a pure dominant plant as the other parent, all the seeds look dominant, as predicted, even though some carry the hidden form.

beats.scene: A page of results with a tick beside every prediction
beats.summary: All the tests agree with the theory, which now stands as Mendel's account of how forms are passed on.

beats.scene: Mendel looks at a pea plant and wonders about two features together
beats.summary: Mendel asks what happens when plants differ in two features at once: do the features travel together or separately?

beats.scene: A plant with round yellow seeds is crossed with one with wrinkled green seeds
beats.summary: He crosses a plant with round yellow seeds with a plant with wrinkled green seeds.

beats.scene: Pods filled with round yellow seeds hang on a hybrid plant
beats.summary: All the first-generation seeds are round and yellow, the two dominant forms.

beats.scene: Fifteen hybrid plants stand in a row, each with pods full of mixed seeds
beats.summary: He grows the seeds into 15 hybrid plants, lets them fertilise themselves, and harvests 556 seeds.

beats.scene: Four heaps of seeds: round yellow, wrinkled yellow, round green, wrinkled green
beats.summary: The 556 seeds fall into four groups: 315 round yellow, 101 wrinkled yellow, 108 round green and 32 wrinkled green.

beats.scene: Two new seed combinations stand out among the four heaps
beats.summary: Two of the four groups are new combinations, wrinkled yellow and round green, which neither grandparent had: the features have been shuffled.

beats.scene: A wall chart shows two separate counts: round to wrinkled and yellow to green
beats.summary: Taken alone, each feature still gives three to one: 423 round to 133 wrinkled, and 416 yellow to 140 green.

beats.scene: Four heaps of seeds sit in the proportion nine, three, three and one
beats.summary: The four groups are in a ratio near 9 : 3 : 3 : 1: for 556 seeds, theory gives about 313, 104, 104 and 35.

beats.scene: Two boxes of three-to-one are drawn multiplied into a grid
beats.summary: Why nine, three, three and one? Three to one multiplied by three to one gives nine, three, three and one.

beats.scene: Two dials turn separately, one for seed shape and one for seed colour
beats.summary: This is Mendel's second great finding: each pair of features is passed on independently of the other pairs.

beats.scene: A hybrid plant releases four kinds of coloured dots as pollen
beats.summary: In Mendel's letters the double hybrid is AaBb, and it makes four kinds of pollen and egg cells, AB, Ab, aB and ab, in equal numbers.

beats.scene: A grid of sixteen squares drawn on a page
beats.summary: Four kinds of pollen meeting four kinds of egg cells give sixteen possible pairings, which can be drawn as a square.

beats.scene: A grid of sixteen squares with four colour groups shaded in
beats.summary: Counting the boxes, nine give round yellow seeds, three give wrinkled yellow, three give round green and one gives wrinkled green.

beats.scene: A garden bed holds many different mixed kinds of pea plant
beats.summary: Behind the four appearances there are nine different kinds of plant, because some look the same but carry different hidden forms.

beats.scene: Mendel sows round yellow seeds, each in its own labelled spot
beats.summary: To test this, he sows 301 of the round yellow seeds and watches what each one grows into.

beats.scene: Four groups of plants stand in the garden in very different numbers
beats.summary: The result: 38 plants give only round yellow seeds, 65 give round yellow and round green, 60 give round yellow and wrinkled yellow, and 138 give all four kinds.

beats.scene: A plan of nine kinds of plant is divided into one, two, two, four
beats.summary: The theory predicts one, two, two and four: only one in nine is pure for both features, and four in nine are double hybrids.

beats.scene: Wrinkled yellow seeds are sown in two rows with different results
beats.summary: The wrinkled yellow seeds also test his idea: 28 plants give only wrinkled yellow seeds and 68 give wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green.

beats.scene: Round green seeds are sown beside wrinkled green seeds
beats.summary: The round green seeds give 35 pure plants and 67 mixed ones, and all the wrinkled green seeds breed true.

beats.scene: A neat table lists every combination of two pairs of features
beats.summary: Mendel sums up: a hybrid forms cells of every possible combination of its features, and each combination is made equally often.

beats.scene: Three small tags of different colours are tied to a single pea plant
beats.summary: Mendel next crosses plants that differ in three pairs of features: seed shape, seed colour and the colour of the seed coat.

beats.scene: Eight kinds of pollen are drawn as eight tiny dots in a ring
beats.summary: With three pairs, a hybrid makes eight kinds of cells, and the plants of the next generation can look like eight different kinds.

beats.scene: A crowded garden bed holds many different mixed kinds of pea plant
beats.summary: These eight appearances hide 27 different kinds of plant, and Mendel's counts agree with the rule.

beats.scene: A table shows four pairs of features and sixteen different looks
beats.summary: With four pairs, a hybrid makes sixteen kinds of cells and there are 81 kinds of plant.

beats.scene: A short ladder of steps, each step doubling the number above it
beats.summary: Mendel gives the general rule: each new pair of features doubles the kinds of cells and multiplies the kinds of plant by three.

beats.scene: A tall ladder of seven steps, each step doubling the number of plant kinds
beats.summary: With all seven pairs, a hybrid makes 128 kinds of cells, and its offspring could include 2,187 kinds of plant.

beats.scene: Many pea plants of different sizes and colours grow in tidy rows

B1B2: Gregor Mendel was a monk who lived in the town of Brünn, which is now Brno in the Czech Republic. In the monastery garden, he began a long series of experiments with plants.
Mendel was born in 1822 in the village of Heinzendorf, where his family farmed a small piece of land. As a boy he learned to look after fruit trees and flowers in the family garden.
The village teacher saw that the boy learned very quickly. He sent him to a better school in the town of Troppau when Mendel was about eleven.
The family had little money, and the school fees were hard to pay. His younger sister Theresia gave him part of her own savings so that he could go on studying.
Mendel went on to study philosophy, mathematics and physics at a college in Olomouc. Money was still short, and he sometimes became ill from worry and overwork.
In 1843 he joined the Augustinian monastery in Brünn, where the monks were also teachers and scholars. There he was given the new name of Gregor, as monks often were.
The abbot, Cyril Napp, liked science and encouraged his monks to study it. The monastery had a good library, a collection of plants and rocks, and a large garden.
Mendel taught the younger boys at a school in the town, and they liked him very much. In 1850, however, he failed the examination that would have made him a full teacher.
From 1851 to 1853 Mendel studied at the University of Vienna. He learned physics from Christian Doppler and the science of plants from Franz Unger.
In 1853 Mendel returned to Brünn and began to teach at the school there. In his free hours he began to wonder how plants pass their features on to their young.
People have always noticed that children look like their parents, and that young animals and plants do too. Farmers have chosen the best ones for breeding for thousands of years.
Around Brünn, farmers wanted better wool from their sheep and better fruit from their trees. They argued about which parents to choose, because nobody knew the rules.
Many people believed that the features of two parents simply blend in their young. It was like mixing red and white paint to make pink.
A hybrid is the young plant that grows from a cross between two different kinds. Gardeners made hybrids by hand because they wanted new colours and shapes in their flowers.
Around 1760 the German botanist Kölreuter crossed tobacco plants with great care. He showed that both parents have a share in the young plant.
Kölreuter also noticed that it did not matter which parent gave the pollen. The young plants looked the same whichever way the cross was made.
Later, the German botanist Carl Gärtner made many thousands of crosses with hundreds of kinds of plant. His work was very careful, but he did not find a simple law.
Some English growers had crossed peas long before Mendel did. They had seen a feature disappear in one generation and then return in the next.
Mendel read the work of these earlier breeders carefully. He saw that they had looked at whole plants, but nobody had counted the young plants one feature at a time.
Mendel wanted to find out the law by which hybrids are formed. He knew that this would take years of patient work with thousands of plants.
Mendel knew that the choice of plant was very important. He wrote that it must meet three needs, and he listed them one by one.
First, the plant must have clear differences between its varieties. These differences must be passed on unchanged, year after year, when the plants are bred among themselves.
Second, the flowers of the hybrids must be guarded from stray pollen. If a bee carried in pollen from another plant, the whole experiment would be spoiled.
Third, the hybrids and their young must be fertile. Otherwise there would be no seeds to sow, and the experiment could not go on for generations.
The pea belongs to the family of legumes, which also includes beans. Its flower has a boat-shaped part, called the keel, that wraps around the parts that make pollen and seed.
The pollen is shed inside the closed flower, often before the bud has opened. So the pea normally fertilises itself, and no visitor can bring in pollen from outside.
Because of this, pea varieties stay pure from year to year. Any change in the young plants would therefore come from his own crosses and not from chance visitors.
Mendel bought 34 different kinds of pea from seed dealers. He sowed them all, because he needed to know which ones were really steady.
Mendel tested all of the varieties in his garden for two full years. Only 22 of them always bred true, and those were the ones that he kept.
In the garden, Mendel tied the tall plants to sticks so that the wind could not knock them down. He also watched for the pea beetle, because it can spoil the seeds.
Mendel decided to use only differences that were sharp and clear. Differences of “more or less” were too hard to measure, so he left them alone.
The first pair of features is the shape of the ripe seed. A seed is either round and smooth, or angular and deeply wrinkled.
The second pair of features is the colour of the seed itself. It shows through the thin seed coat, so a seed is either yellow or green.
The third pair is the colour of the seed coat, which is either grey-brown or white. It goes with the flowers, because plants with white seeds have white flowers.
The fourth pair is the shape of the ripe pod. A pod is either full and smoothly curved, or pinched in tightly between the seeds.
The fifth pair is the colour of the unripe pod, which is either some shade of green or a bright yellow. The yellow colour also shows on the stalks and the veins of the leaves.
The sixth pair is the position of the flowers. They grow either along the main stem, or in a bunch at the very top.
The seventh pair is the length of the stem. The tall plants are about six or seven feet high, while the short ones are less than two feet.
In all, Mendel had seven pairs of features to follow. For each pair, a plant showed one form or the other, and never something in between.
The experiments lasted about eight years and used many thousands of plants. Mendel counted every one of them by hand, so the numbers in his paper are real.
Mendel needed only a few small tools to make a cross. He used fine tweezers, a soft brush, little bags and paper labels.
First, Mendel chose a young flower that was still closed. With great care, he opened the keel so that he could reach the parts inside.
Next, he removed all the anthers with tweezers before they were ripe. Without them, the flower could not make seeds with its own pollen.
Then he collected ripe pollen from the plant he had chosen and brushed it onto the pistil. The tip of the pistil is slightly sticky, so the grains held fast.
Finally, he tied a small bag over the flower. This kept out insects and wind, so that no other pollen could reach the pistil.

Peas flower for only a few weeks each spring. Mendel had to move quickly along the rows, because every flower needed attention at just the right moment.

The first generation had looked simple, but it had raised a serious question. Where had the hidden form gone, and could it ever come back?
The next spring, Mendel planted the hybrid seeds in tidy rows. He let the new plants fertilise themselves and waited for their pods to ripen.
When Mendel opened the pods, he found both round and wrinkled seeds. The hidden form had not been destroyed, because it had been waiting inside the hybrid.
Mendel counted all the seeds from the hybrid plants. There were 5,474 round seeds and 1,850 wrinkled ones, which is nearly three round for every wrinkled seed.

The length of the stem gave 787 tall plants and 277 short ones. Here the short plants were a little more than one quarter of the whole.

The numbers were close to three to one, but they were never exactly so. Mendel does not hide the small differences, and he prints every figure.
Think of a coin that is tossed only ten times in a row. It may not give exactly five heads, but with thousands of tosses the heads come close to half of the total.
A single pod has only a handful of seeds in it. Such a small group can show almost any ratio, so it cannot show the real one.
So Mendel added up the counts from all of the plants together. As the total grew larger, the ratio settled closer and closer to three to one.
The shape and colour of the seed can be seen in the seeds themselves. Features of the plant, such as its height, only show after the seeds have been sown, so they take a year longer.
Mendel now asked a new question that went a step deeper than before. Was the hidden form still the same as before, or had its time inside the hybrid changed it?
In the next spring, Mendel sowed the seeds of each plant in a separate row. In this way he could follow every family on its own.
The plants grown from wrinkled seeds gave only wrinkled seeds, in every row. The hidden form had returned just as pure as before.
The same was true for green seeds and for all the other hidden forms. Wherever the hidden form came back, it stayed pure for ever after.
The plants with the dominant form were not so simple. Some of them behaved one way and some another, and Mendel wanted to understand why.
Mendel took more than five hundred plants with the dominant form, for each of two features. He sowed a number of seeds from every one of them, to see what they would give.
Some of these plants gave only round seeds, so they were pure. Others gave round and wrinkled seeds together, so they were hybrids, just like the first generation.
For the shape of the seed, Mendel tested 565 plants with round seeds. Of these plants, 193 gave only round seeds, and 372 gave both kinds, which is about one to two.
The test with seed colour gave the same kind of answer. Of 519 plants, 166 gave only yellow seeds and 353 gave yellow and green seeds together.
When Mendel counted the seeds of the mixed plants, he found the old ratio again. Once more, there were about three round seeds for each wrinkled one.
So the three-to-one ratio was hiding a ratio of one to two to one. One quarter of the plants were pure dominant, half were hybrids and one quarter were pure recessive.
Mendel did not stop with only two of the features. He tested all seven pairs, and the pattern of one to two to one held in every one of them.
Mendel's work shows that a plant can look like one parent and still carry the hidden form of the other. How a living thing looks does not tell us everything about what it carries.
Mendel followed the families for several more generations in a row. In each one, only half of the offspring of a hybrid were hybrids again, while the other half bred true.
Mendel worked out what this meant over ten generations. Among 2,048 plants, there would be 1,023 pure plants of each form, and only two hybrids.
To show the pattern very clearly, Mendel decided to use letters instead of words. He wrote a large A for the dominant form and a small a for the hidden form, so that a hybrid became Aa.
In this shorthand, the second generation was written A plus two Aa plus a. That means one pure dominant plant, two hybrids and one pure recessive plant.
Mendel guessed that a hybrid makes two kinds of pollen cells and two kinds of egg cells. Each cell carries only one form, either the dominant one or the hidden one.
A pure plant is different from a hybrid, because it carries the same form twice. It can make only one kind of pollen and one kind of egg cell.
Which pollen cell meets which egg cell is a matter of pure chance. It is like drawing one marble from each of two bags, with half of each colour in both.
There are four possible pairings: A with A, A with a, a with A, and a with a. Each of them is equally likely, so each should turn up about once in four times.
In three of the four pairings, the dominant form is present, so it shows. Only in the fourth pairing, a with a, can the hidden form appear.
The pairings also explain the ratio of one to two to one. A with A gives a pure dominant plant, two mixed pairings give hybrids, and a with a gives a pure recessive plant.
The key point of Mendel's explanation is that the two forms never blend. Inside a hybrid they stay separate, and they are sorted into different cells when the next generation begins.
Mendel could not see any of this happening inside the flowers. He reached his explanation by reasoning from the numbers alone, which was a bold step.
A good explanation must predict something that nobody has seen yet. Mendel looked for a test that would show his idea to be wrong, if it was.
His first test was to cross a hybrid with a pure plant of the hidden form. The theory said that half of the young should be hybrids and half pure.
The second test crossed a hybrid with a pure plant of the dominant form. The theory said that every young plant would look dominant, but half of them would still be hybrids inside.
To make the test sharper, Mendel followed two features at once. For this test, his theory predicted four groups of equal size instead of two.
Mendel fertilised flowers of hybrid plants with pollen from a plant with wrinkled green seeds. Then he waited for the pods and sorted all the seeds into groups.

The four groups came out almost equal: 31 round yellow, 26 round green, 27 wrinkled yellow and 26 wrinkled green. The prediction of four equal groups had come true, and the theory had passed its test.
Mendel then reversed the cross, so that the hybrid gave the pollen and the other plant gave the egg cells. The four groups of seeds were again almost equal in number, with 24, 25, 22 and 26.
This showed that the hybrid makes all four kinds of cells in equal numbers. It does this both in its pollen and in its egg cells.
When the other parent was a pure plant of the dominant form, every seed showed the dominant form. This matched the prediction, although some seeds secretly carried the hidden form.
Every test agreed with Mendel's idea, and so the idea grew stronger. It was no longer only a guess but a well-tested explanation.
Until now, Mendel had followed one pair of features at a time. Now he asked what would happen when plants differ in two pairs at once.
Mendel crossed a plant that had round yellow seeds with a plant that had wrinkled green seeds. One parent showed both dominant forms, and the other showed both hidden forms.
All the first-generation seeds were round and yellow, which are the two dominant forms. That was just what the earlier results had led him to expect.
Mendel grew the hybrid seeds into plants and let them fertilise themselves. The pods of fifteen plants gave a harvest of 556 seeds.

The 556 seeds fell into four distinct groups of very different sizes, which Mendel counted carefully. There were 315 round yellow seeds, 101 wrinkled yellow seeds, 108 round green seeds and 32 wrinkled green seeds.
Two of the four groups were new combinations: wrinkled yellow seeds and round green seeds. Neither of the grandparents had looked like that, so the features had been shuffled.
Taken alone, each feature still gave three to one. There were 423 round seeds to 133 wrinkled ones, and 416 yellow seeds to 140 green ones.
The four groups came remarkably close to the ratio of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. For 556 seeds, that ratio gives about 313, 104, 104 and 35, so the actual counts were very near the prediction.

The reason for this pattern is simple, because it is just a matter of multiplication. One three-to-one pattern combined with another gives three times three, three times one, one times three and one times one.
This was Mendel's second great finding, and it is still taught in schools. Each pair of features is inherited independently of the other pairs, like two dials that turn separately.
In Mendel's letters, the hybrid for both pairs of features is written AaBb. It makes four kinds of pollen and four kinds of egg cells, called AB, Ab, aB and ab, in equal numbers.
Four kinds of pollen can meet four kinds of egg cells, which makes sixteen possible pairings. Today we draw them as a square of sixteen boxes, a method invented later by Reginald Punnett.
Counting the boxes, we find that nine of the sixteen show round yellow seeds. Three show wrinkled yellow, three show round green, and only one shows wrinkled green.
Behind the four appearances, there are nine different kinds of plants. Some seeds look exactly alike, but they carry different hidden forms inside.
To test this idea, Mendel planted 301 of the round yellow seeds, each in its own place. He then waited to see what kind of plant each one would make.

The 301 plants split into four groups of very different sizes, which Mendel counted with care. Thirty-eight gave only round yellow seeds, 65 gave round yellow and round green, 60 gave round yellow and wrinkled yellow, and 138 gave all four kinds.
His idea predicted these proportions in advance, as one, two, two and four. The double hybrids are the largest group of all, at four in every nine round yellow seeds.
The wrinkled yellow seeds were tested in the same way. About one third of the plants bred true, and the other two thirds gave wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green seeds.
The round green seeds gave 35 pure plants and 67 mixed ones, again about one to two. The wrinkled green seeds, which carry both hidden forms, bred true in every case.
Mendel summed up the result in a clear sentence. A hybrid forms cells of every possible combination of its features, and each combination is made equally often.
Next, Mendel crossed plants that differ in three pairs of features at once. These were the shape of the seed, its colour, and the colour of the seed coat.
With three pairs of features, a hybrid makes eight kinds of cells in equal numbers. The plants of the next generation can look like eight different kinds.
The eight kinds of looks hide 27 different kinds of plants underneath. Mendel's counts agreed well with the rule, even with so many groups.
With four pairs of features, a hybrid makes sixteen kinds of cells. The next generation can include 81 different kinds of plant.
Mendel then found a general rule that works for any number of pairs of features. Each new pair of features doubles the number of kinds of cells and multiplies the number of kinds of plants by three.
With all seven pairs of features, a hybrid would make 128 kinds of cells. The next generation could then include 2,187 different kinds of plants.
This helps to explain something that everybody has noticed in their own family. A few simple rules can make an enormous number of different offspring, even from the same two parents.
Mendel did not test only one combination of features, but several different ones. Every one of the combinations followed the same rule, as far as he could tell.
Because the features are shuffled, the crosses made new pure varieties of pea. Round green and wrinkled yellow peas now bred true, and neither parent had looked like that.
By now Mendel had a clear rule for peas. He wondered whether other plants would follow it, so he turned to beans.
Mendel also crossed two different kinds of bean in the same garden. One was a tall runner with red flowers, and the other was a short bean with white flowers.
The bean flowers gave a much more complicated result than the peas had done. The second generation showed many different shades of colour, not just two.
Mendel suggested a clever answer to this puzzle of the many shades. He thought that the flower colour of the bean was made by several separate pairs of features working together.
Later scientists showed that Mendel had been right to suspect a team of factors. Many features, such as the height of a person, depend on many genes working together.
Some plants do not follow the pea pattern of dominance. When a red marvel of Peru is crossed with a white one, the young plants have pink flowers.
Earlier breeders had seen that hybrids sometimes went back to look like their parents. Mendel's rule explains this, because the pure parent forms come back in the next generations.
In his closing remarks, Mendel asked what hybrids might tell us about how new forms arise. He stayed cautious, however, and he claimed no more than his plants had shown.
Mendel used mathematics to study living things, which was very unusual in biology at that time. His training in physics and mathematics helped him to see patterns in numbers.
Mendel's method can be put in a few words. He chose clear features, he crossed plants under control, he followed every generation, and he counted everything.
Mendel wrote up his work as a long and careful paper. It was written in plain language, and it was full of tables that anyone could check.
Mendel was a member of the Natural History Society of Brünn. Its members were teachers, doctors and other townspeople who loved to study nature in their free time.
On 8 February 1865, Mendel read the first part of his paper to the Society. He described his peas and the results of the first crosses.
The listeners were polite, but they did not seem to understand what they had heard. Accounts of the evening suggest that there was very little discussion.
A month later, on 8 March, Mendel gave the second part of his talk. In it he explained his theory and showed the combinations of letters.
The paper was printed in 1866 in the journal of the Society. Its title meant Experiments on Plant Hybrids, and it ran to more than forty pages.
The journal was sent to scientific societies and libraries in many countries. Mendel also had a few dozen separate copies of his own paper printed, to send to scientists.
For many years after it was printed, hardly anybody mentioned the paper at all. When it was cited at all, it was seen as one more study of pea hybrids.
Mendel wrote to Carl Nägeli, a leading botanist in Munich. He sent a copy of the paper and asked for an expert opinion.
Nägeli replied politely, but he was not convinced by the results. He advised Mendel to try the hawkweed, a plant that he himself was studying.
The hawkweed hybrids did not follow the rules of the peas. Mendel reported this in 1869, but the reason was unknown to him, and it was found only later.
His main pea experiments had run from about 1856 to 1863. In later years, Mendel turned to other studies, such as bees and the weather.
In 1870 a strong whirlwind crossed the town of Brünn. Mendel studied the damage and wrote a careful report on how it had moved.

As abbot, Mendel had much less time for experiments. He gave up his plant crosses little by little and turned to other duties.

People who knew Mendel remembered him as a kind man. He was generous to the poor and he helped students who had little money, as his sister had once helped him.
Mendel became ill in his last years, and he died in January 1884 at the age of 61. A kidney illness was the cause of his death.
After Mendel's death, many of his private papers were burned. This is why historians know less about his work than they would like.
One of Mendel's friends later recalled that he had said, “My time will come.” We cannot be sure of the exact words, but they have become famous.
In those years, Charles Darwin had shown that living things change over time. He had no good explanation, however, for how features are passed from parents to young.
In the spring of 1900, three scientists in different countries found the same pattern in their own experiments. They had worked separately, but their results agreed with each other very closely.
Hugo de Vries in the Netherlands had crossed many kinds of plants. In March 1900 he was the first of the three to publish his results.
Carl Correns in Germany had worked with peas and maize. After he reached the same results, he found Mendel's old paper and was astonished to see that it had all been done before.
Erich von Tschermak in Austria had also crossed peas, and he soon published results of the same kind. Historians still disagree about how well he understood them.
All three scientists agreed that Mendel had done it first. His forgotten paper was suddenly read by scientists in many countries.

Peas have seven pairs of chromosomes, and Mendel studied seven features. They lie on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one, so they sorted independently.

A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries instructions for making part of a living thing. The two forms that Mendel followed are two versions of the same instruction.
In 1990, more than a century after Mendel's paper, scientists found the gene behind wrinkled peas. A change in it alters how the seed stores starch and sugar.

In 1936 the statistician Ronald Fisher said that some of Mendel's counts were closer to the expected ratios than chance usually allows. Historians still debate the reasons, but other people have repeated his experiments with the same results.
Today, pupils all over the world still grow peas and count them in school. They are often surprised when their own numbers come close to three to one.
Mendel's two main findings are now called the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment. Every student of biology learns about them early in the course, and they are still used today.
Farmers and breeders use Mendel's ideas to make better crops and animals. They choose the parents on purpose, so that good features are brought together.
Doctors and genetic counsellors use these rules to explain how some conditions run in families. They can say what the chances are, although real life is often more complicated than peas.
Today, visitors can see Mendel's old monastery in Brno, where there is a museum about his life. In 2022, many countries marked the two hundredth anniversary of his birth.
Mendel's paper is also a lesson in honesty and in modesty for every scientist. He reported what he had seen, he said where he was unsure, and he left the rest for others to work out.
In the same way, each of us carries a mixture of features from both of our parents. Chance shuffles these features, so we resemble our families and yet we are different.
In 2003, scientists announced that they had read nearly all of the human genome, which is about three billion letters long. That huge book of instructions grew from questions like Mendel's.
Over the years, scientists have found the genes behind several of Mendel's seven features. In 2019 the complete genome of the pea was published, so his plant has now been read from end to end.
Mendel's garden was small, and his tools were simple: a brush, a notebook and a great deal of patience. With them, he found a law of nature that still helps us to understand every living thing.

Johann Mendel, who would later take the name Gregor, was born in 1822 into a hard-working farming family in the village of Heinzendorf in Silesia. From his father he learned how to graft young fruit trees, and he grew up watching how plants behave from season to season. The habit of looking closely at living things stayed with him all his life.

The village teacher soon noticed that the farmer's son learned faster than anyone else, and he persuaded the family to send him on to a better school in the nearby town of Troppau. It was a great change for a country boy, because it meant leaving home and living among strangers. Yet he worked hard and did well, and the road to a life of study was now open to him.

When an accident to his father left the family short of money, the fees for the next school seemed impossible to find. His younger sister Theresia then gave up part of the savings that she had put aside for her marriage, so that her brother could go on learning. Years later he repaid her kindness by helping to pay for the education of her sons.

Money was still short, and the strain of poverty and constant study at times made him ill. He needed a way of life that would let him learn without always counting the cost.

In 1843 the young man entered the Augustinian monastery in Brünn, where the monks were expected to teach and to study as well as to pray. He took the name Gregor, and with it he gained a quiet home, a library and a steady life. It was not a life of adventure, but it gave him time to think.

The abbot, Cyril Napp, believed that learning was part of a monk's duty, and he welcomed new ideas in farming and in science. The monastery therefore held a fine library, collections of plants and minerals, and a large garden where experiments could be tried. For a curious young monk with a questioning mind, it was a very good place to be.

Mendel soon proved to be a gifted teacher of the young, and his pupils remembered him kindly. In 1850, however, he failed the examination that would have made him a fully qualified teacher, a disappointment that might have ended another man's hopes. The abbot did not give up on him, but sent him away to study further.

He also learned to think in numbers and to test an idea by experiment, habits that would serve him well in the garden. It was the most complete scientific training that he would ever receive, and he used it well for the rest of his life.

Back in Brünn in 1853, Mendel taught physics and natural history at the local school, and he was still a monk in the monastery. In his free hours he kept returning to a single question: how does a plant pass its features on to its young? Before long that single question would fill a corner of the monastery garden with row upon row of peas.

Everyone has noticed that children resemble their parents, and the same is true of young animals and young plants. For thousands of years farmers have used this fact, choosing the strongest animals and the best seed to produce the next generation. What they could not explain was how a feature passes from one life to the next.

In the lands around Brünn, farmers and fruit growers were eager to improve their sheep, their wool and their orchards. The abbot and some monks of Mendel's own monastery took part in these discussions.

A common belief of the time was that the features of two parents blend in their offspring, much as red paint and white paint blend into pink. If that were true, however, it would be hard to see why a grandchild sometimes resembles a grandparent more than a parent. The old idea of blending explained a few things well enough, but it left many puzzles quite unsolved.

A hybrid is the offspring of two parents that differ in some way, and in the nineteenth century gardeners were making hybrids of ornamental plants in great numbers. His careful work proved that plants could be studied by experiment, like any other living things in nature.

Peas had been crossed before, for English growers such as Thomas Knight and John Goss had tried it a generation earlier. They noticed with surprise that a feature could vanish in the first young plants and then come back in the next. But they only noted it, and they did not count how often it happened.

Reading the work of the earlier breeders with great care, Mendel saw clearly what was missing from it. They had compared whole plants, which differ in a hundred ways at once, and so the patterns were lost in the crowd. Nobody had followed a single feature through the generations and counted every plant that showed it.

Mendel set himself a clear goal: to discover the general law by which hybrid plants are formed and by which their features pass to the next generation. He knew that the task was a large one that could only be settled by long, patient work on a very great number of plants. The man who would succeed, he saw, must be willing to count, to wait and to repeat his work many times.

Mendel understood that the success of the whole project depended on choosing the right plant. The first condition is that the plant should have differing features that are clear and constant. A tall variety must always give tall plants, and a short variety must always give short ones, when each is bred only with its own kind. The second condition is that the flowers of the hybrid plants must be protected from foreign pollen, or at least easy to protect. If a bee or a breeze delivered the wrong grains at the wrong moment, a result would be false and the careful work of a whole season would be wasted. Mendel's whole plan therefore depended on finding a flower that could be kept private from every visitor.

The third condition is that the hybrids, and their descendants, must not lose their fertility to any marked degree. Many hybrids of different species are weak or sterile, and an experiment that dies out after one generation can reveal nothing about the long run. Mendel needed plants that would go on producing healthy seeds for many years, generation after generation, without any weakness.

The garden pea belongs to the legume family, whose members also include beans, clover and lentils. Its flower has a curious structure: two lower petals form a boat-shaped keel that encloses both the pollen-bearing anthers and the pistil, which will become the pod. Because everything is shut inside, the flower works almost like a small closed room.

In the pea the pollen is shed and settles on the pistil while the flower is still closed, often before the bud has opened at all. The plant therefore fertilises itself, which is exactly what Mendel wanted, because it protects the flower from stray pollen. A pea that keeps its own pollen is an ideal subject for a careful experiment.

Because the flowers fertilise themselves, the varieties of pea stay pure from one year to the next, with each one passing on its own features unchanged. Any surprise that appeared in the young plants could therefore be traced to a cross that Mendel had made himself. That clarity is one of the greatest strengths of his choice of plant, and it made every later result easier to trust.

To begin, Mendel obtained 34 varieties of pea from several seed dealers, and he planted them side by side in his garden.
