For two years Mendel watched the 34 varieties, searching for any that wavered in their features from one season to the next. Twenty-two of them passed the test and bred true, so he kept those and set the others aside. It was slow, careful work, and it was only the preparation for the experiments themselves.

In the garden beds Mendel tied the tall plants to stakes to keep them upright in the wind, and he kept a close eye on the pea beetle, a small pest that can eat into the seeds. Every detail of the plot was arranged so that nothing could disturb the results. It is this attention to small things that makes the later numbers so trustworthy.

Mendel decided to use only the differences that were sharp and unmistakable, such as a seed that is either round or wrinkled. Features that differ merely by degrees, in the manner of “more or less”, are hard to count and easy to argue about, so he set them aside. A plant either has a feature or it does not, and that made the counting possible.

The first pair concerns the shape of the ripe seed, which is either round, or irregularly angular and deeply wrinkled. Mendel could tell the two apart at a glance, even after the peas had dried, and so a large heap of seeds could be sorted without any doubt or argument. Because the difference was so clear, a whole pile of seeds could be counted in a single evening.

The second pair is the colour of the seed's inner substance, which shows through the thin skin and is either pale yellow, or some shade of green. Mendel found that this feature, like the shape of the seed, could be judged without growing a single plant. It was simply a matter of opening a pod in the late summer and looking carefully at what was inside.

The third pair is the colour of the seed coat, which is either grey, grey-brown or leather-brown, or else white. Mendel noticed that this feature travels together with the colour of the flower, for the white seeds always grow into plants with white blossoms, while the dark seeds grow into plants with purple-red ones. The flowers were therefore a second and quite separate way of reading the same feature in the growing plant.

The fourth pair is the shape of the ripe pod, which is either full and smoothly curved or deeply pinched in between the seeds. The difference is easy to see, and it concerns a part of the plant quite separate from the seed itself. Mendel wanted features that seemed to have nothing at all to do with one another, so that each could be followed alone.

The fifth pair is the colour of the pod before it ripens, which is either light to dark green or a vivid yellow. The yellow plants also show a yellowish tinge in the stalks, the calyx and the veins of the leaves, so that the difference reaches into more than the pod alone. In a garden bed, the two kinds stood out like lamps among the leaves.

The sixth pair is the position of the flowers, which in some plants are scattered along the length of the main stem and in others are bunched together at its top. The two arrangements give the plants quite different outlines, though the flowers themselves look much the same. Mendel counted each of the two arrangements as one clear feature, with nothing in between them to cause doubt.

The seventh pair is the length of the stem, and the contrast is dramatic: the tall plants reach about six or seven feet, while the short ones stay below about two. Mendel chose varieties with such a clear gap between them that no plant could be mistaken for the other kind. A feature that cannot be argued about is a feature that can be counted.

In all, Mendel now had seven pairs of features, and in each pair a plant showed the one form or the other with no halfway cases. The seven pairs concerned the seed, the pod, the flower and the stem, so he was watching the whole plant at once. It was a bold and demanding plan, and it was one that would richly reward a patient man.

The experiments went on for about eight years, from the first sowing to the last count, and they involved many thousands of plants. Every plant and every seed was examined by hand and written down, so that the figures in the paper are real counts and not estimates. It is hard for anyone today to imagine the patience that this long and quiet work demanded of him.

Crossing peas by hand required only a few small tools, but it required great delicacy of touch as well. Mendel used fine tweezers, a soft brush, little bags and paper labels, and he kept them close at hand for each day's work. Everything depended on steady fingers, good light and a quiet morning in the garden before the day grew warm.

The first step was to choose a young flower that had not yet opened, and then to part the keel with the greatest gentleness. A single clumsy movement could tear the delicate petals or spoil the flower altogether. Inside the keel, the tiny parts of the flower waited, pale and fresh and still quite unripe.

Next came the most delicate task of all: removing every one of the anthers with the tweezers before the pollen had ripened. A flower treated in this way could no longer fertilise itself, so that it would accept only the pollen that Mendel chose to give it. If he waited a single day too long, the pollen would already have been shed and the work would be spoiled.

Then he gathered ripe pollen from the plant he had selected as the father and brushed it onto the tip of the pistil, which is slightly sticky and holds the grains firmly. From that moment, the pollen grains would begin to grow down toward the egg cells waiting below. The cross was now made, but only the long months of summer would show what it had produced.

Finally, he covered the flower with a small bag to keep out insects and drifting pollen. The precaution was a simple one, but it meant that the seeds that followed could have only two parents, and both were known to him. Without such a bag the experiment would have meant nothing, because no one could have said who the parents were.

Every crossed flower received a label, and every label was copied into a notebook, so that Mendel could always say which parents had made which pods. Months might pass between the cross and the count, and a lost label could mean a lost result. Good records were quite as much a part of the experiment as the plants and the pollen themselves.

Mendel made every cross in both directions, so that each kind of plant served once as the pollen parent and once as the seed parent. He wanted to know whether the father and the mother contributed differently to the young. Whether the direction of a cross mattered was something he would check at once.

To raise the next generation, Mendel did not need his tweezers and his brush at all. He simply let the hybrid plants fertilise themselves in the natural way, as peas have always done, and then gathered their seeds. The pea's closed flower, which was such a nuisance for crossing, now saved him a great deal of work.

The peas bloom for only a few weeks each year, and in that short season Mendel had to make all of his crosses. Every flower had to be reached at precisely the right stage, so that the days in the garden were long, careful and tiring. A missed week could mean waiting a whole year for another chance, and Mendel had no wish to waste a season.

As summer ended and the pods dried, Mendel opened each one in turn, counted its seeds and sorted them according to their features. The seeds were then stored in labelled packets until the following spring, when they would be sown to grow the next generation. Each small packet held one piece of an answer that Mendel could not yet see as a whole.

Mendel began with the shape of the seed, joining plants that bore round seeds to plants that bore wrinkled ones. All he could do then was wait while the flowers faded and the pods swelled, and the wait must have felt very long. The first answer would not come until the pods had ripened and were opened, late in the summer.

When Mendel opened the pods, he found that every single seed was round, with not one wrinkled seed among them. A mixture of the two parents, with slightly wrinkled seeds, might have seemed natural, but nothing of the kind had happened. The wrinkled form had vanished from the pods without leaving a trace, at least for the moment.

The result was repeated when Mendel turned his attention to the colour of the seed. Plants with yellow seeds crossed with plants with green seeds produced only yellow seeds, and the green had gone, as the wrinkles had gone before. Evidently something regular was at work, and it was certainly not a simple blend.

Mendel went on to cross the plants for each of the other pairs of features in turn, and the story was always the same. The young plants resembled only one of the two parents, and the other parent's feature could not be found in them at all. Seven different pairs of features had given seven separate examples of one and the same rule.

In each of the seven pairs, one form took over in the first generation, and Mendel could now list them all. Round seeds, yellow seeds, grey-brown seed coats, full pods, green unripe pods, flowers along the stem and tall plants were the winners, while their opposites seemed to have been wiped out. Whether they had really gone was a question that he could not yet answer.

Mendel needed a name for the feature that passes into the hybrid and shows itself there, and he called it the dominant feature. The word suited it well, since it seemed to rule over its partner and to take the whole of the stage. Biologists still use the word today, and every student of heredity meets it early in the course.

The feature that seemed to vanish from the hybrid he called recessive, since it appeared to recede into the background. That was only a first impression, because nobody yet knew whether the hidden form was gone for ever or was merely waiting. The garden in the following season would at last give him a clear and decisive answer to the question.

When Mendel compared the crosses made in the two directions, he found that the results were identical in every case. It made no difference whether the dominant form came with the pollen or with the egg cell, and this was a clear sign that father and mother have an equal share in the young plant. The old idea that one parent counts for more had no support in his garden.

In the pea, the hybrid looks like one of its parents and not like a blend of the two, which was a surprise to anyone who expected the paints to mix. Many other plants, as Kölreuter and others had reported, give hybrids that fall somewhere between the parents. Mendel's peas followed a different and much simpler pattern, and that made the pattern easier to see.

The first generation had looked simple, yet it raised a question that could not be put aside. If the hidden feature had been destroyed, then it should never be seen again, but if it was only waiting, then it should return at some later time. Mendel knew exactly how to find out, and the answer would come with the next harvest.

In the following spring Mendel planted the hybrid seeds in tidy rows, and let the young plants fertilise themselves in the usual way. All through the summer he watched them grow, and then he waited for the pods to ripen. It was the first real test of what had happened to the hidden form, and he knew it well.

When the pods were opened, they held round seeds and wrinkled seeds together, side by side in the same pod. The hidden form had not been destroyed at all, for it had been waiting inside the hybrid plants and had now come back into the open. It was the first great surprise of the whole experiment, and it opened a completely new line of thought.

Mendel counted every single seed from the hybrid plants, and the total came to 7,324 in all. Of these, 5,474 were round and 1,850 were wrinkled, which is nearly three round seeds for every wrinkled one. The pattern was unmistakable, and it seemed far too regular to be the product of mere accident.

The colour of the seed told exactly the same story as the shape had told, and told it just as clearly. From the hybrid plants Mendel gathered 8,023 seeds, of which 6,022 were yellow and 2,001 were green, a ratio so close to three to one that he could hardly doubt it. Two quite different features of the plant had given the very same answer, and the answer was far from random.

The flowers, which go with the colour of the seed coat, gave a similar result. Among the plants of the second generation, 705 bore purple-red blossoms and 224 bore white ones, so that the ratio was a little above three to one. The slight difference from an exact three to one was no cause for worry, since real counts are never perfectly neat.

When he turned to the shape of the pod, Mendel counted 882 plants with full pods and 299 with pinched ones. The ratio was once more very close to three to one, although the plants and the feature were quite different from the ones before. It began to look as though a single rule governed all of these different features in the same quiet way.

The colour of the unripe pods gave 428 plants with green pods and 152 with yellow ones, which was the smallest group that Mendel counted in the whole series. Its ratio came out a little below three to one, which is just what one would expect from a smaller number of plants. Small counts wander further from the true ratio than large ones do, which is exactly why large counts are needed.

In the case of flower position, Mendel found 651 plants with flowers along the stem and 207 with flowers bunched at the top. The ratio was again close to three to one, and each new set of figures made the pattern harder to dismiss. A rule seemed to be taking shape out of the numbers, as a picture appears out of scattered dots.

Last of all, the length of the stem gave 787 tall plants and 277 short ones, so that the short plants made up about a quarter of the total. This was the seventh pair, and the seventh time that the hidden form had come back at roughly the same share. A pattern that appears seven times is very unlikely to be a trick of chance.

Altogether, Mendel counted close to 20,000 seeds and plants in this generation, and he set the seven sets of figures side by side. In every pair of features, the dominant form outnumbered the recessive form by about three to one, within the small differences that chance allows. Seven separate experiments, made on seven quite different features, had given one simple and surprising rule.

None of the ratios was exactly three to one, and Mendel does not pretend otherwise: the figures stand in his paper just as he counted them. Some are a little above the expected value and some a little below, as the numbers of any real count must be. An honest list of small differences is worth far more to a scientist than a list that looks perfect.

A coin tossed ten times will seldom give exactly five heads, because chance makes small samples uneven. Tossed ten thousand times, however, it comes very close to half heads, and the more tosses there are, the closer the share comes to one half. Mendel's peas behaved in the same way, which is why he needed so many of them.

A single pod holds only a handful of seeds, and a single plant only a few dozen, so the ratio in one pod or plant can swing wildly. A scientist who looked at just a few plants might have seen almost any ratio at all and given up the search for a rule. Only very large numbers allow the true pattern to rise clearly above the noise of chance.

So Mendel added together the counts from all the plants, row by row and bed by bed, and watched the true ratio emerge from the confusion. The sums were long and the writing was small, but each added line made the answer a little more certain. In this way, long months of patience were slowly turned into firm and lasting scientific evidence.

The shape and colour of a seed can be read from the seed itself, so those counts could be made as soon as the pods were opened. Features of the plant, such as its height or the place of its flowers, appear only after the seeds are sown and have grown, which costs a whole extra year. Mendel had to keep his rows, his labels and his years straight in his mind at all times.

Mendel now put a sharper question to the plants: was the hidden form still the same as before, or had it been altered during its time inside the hybrid? To answer it, he would have to raise the descendants of each second-generation plant and watch them separately. It was far more work than before, but the answer would be well worth all of the effort.

In the next season, Mendel sowed the seeds of each second-generation plant in a row of its own, labelled with the plant's number. In this way he could follow every family separately, instead of mixing all the offspring into one great heap. The work grew much heavier, but only this method could show what the hidden form was really like.

The plants that had grown from wrinkled seeds gave only wrinkled seeds in every one of the rows, generation after generation. The hidden form had come back just as pure as it had been in the grandparents, without the slightest trace of the dominant form. Its long time in hiding inside the hybrid plants had not changed it in any way at all.

Green seeds behaved in exactly the same way as wrinkled ones, and so did every other recessive form that he followed. Wherever a hidden feature had returned, it now bred true in the plants that carried it, and the next generation showed no trace of its former partner. The recessive form, it seemed, had been kept safe, whole and quite unchanged through its time of hiding.

The plants that showed the dominant form turned out to be less simple than the recessive ones. Although they looked exactly alike, they did not all behave in the same way when their seeds were sown, and Mendel realised that appearances were hiding something. The garden was about to give him a much deeper lesson than any he had learned so far.

For two of the features, shape and colour, Mendel selected more than five hundred plants showing the dominant form, and he sowed a number of seeds from each of them. Since every one of those plants looked the same as the next, only the offspring could reveal which ones were hybrids. It was a large and tiring experiment, and the results that it gave him were truly remarkable.

Some of the plants gave only round seeds in the next generation, and so they were pure. Others gave both round and wrinkled seeds, and again in a ratio near three to one, so that they behaved exactly like the hybrids of the first generation. Two plants that looked absolutely identical had turned out to be quite different on the inside.

For the shape of the seed, he tested 565 plants of the dominant form, and the results fell into two unequal groups. A total of 193 plants gave only round seeds, while 372 gave both round and wrinkled seeds, so that the hybrids outnumbered the pure plants by about two to one. It was a ratio with a meaning, and he was only beginning to see how much it meant.

The test with the colour of the seed gave an answer of exactly the same kind as before. Of the 519 yellow-seeded plants that he examined, 166 produced only yellow seeds and 353 produced yellow and green seeds together, which is again a ratio of about one to two. Two different features had shown the same pattern, and it could no longer be a coincidence.

When he counted the seeds of the mixed plants, Mendel found the old ratio again: about three plants with the dominant form to every one with the recessive form. The hybrids of the second generation were therefore behaving exactly like those of the first, and they were making the same mixture all over again. The process was a cycle that repeated itself again and again, in every generation that followed.

The famous three to one now disclosed the structure that it had been concealing all along, a ratio of one to two to one. One quarter of the second generation were pure plants of the dominant form, one half were hybrids like their parents, and one quarter were pure plants of the recessive form. Three different kinds of plant stood hidden behind only two kinds of outward appearance.

Mendel did not stop with two features, but went on to test the dominant plants of all seven pairs in the same careful way. In every case the plants sorted themselves into pure and hybrid in the ratio of one to two, and the recessive forms stayed pure. The rule, whatever it was, did not depend on which feature he happened to choose.

One of the paper's quiet lessons is that two plants may look exactly alike and yet differ in what they carry within them. A hybrid with round seeds and a pure plant with round seeds are indistinguishable by eye, but their offspring reveal the difference at once. Appearance, in other words, is only the visible half of the story of inheritance.

Mendel followed the families through several more generations, always letting the plants fertilise themselves. Each time, only half of the offspring of a hybrid were hybrids again, while the other half bred true as pure plants of one form or the other. The share of hybrids was therefore cut in half with every new generation that was sown.

Mendel worked out with simple arithmetic what this would mean after ten whole generations of self-fertilisation. Among every 2,048 plants of the tenth generation, 1,023 would be pure plants of the dominant form, another 1,023 would be pure plants of the recessive form, and only two would still be hybrids. In this way the hybrids steadily fade away, and the pure forms take over.

To show the pattern at a glance, Mendel used simple letters instead of long descriptions in words. A capital A stood for the dominant form, a small a for the recessive form, and the pair Aa for a hybrid that carried both. The shorthand was simple, yet it turned a tangle of seeds and plants into something that could be calculated.

In the same shorthand, the second generation was written as A plus two Aa plus a, which means one pure dominant plant, two hybrids and one pure recessive plant. That short line carries the whole result of the counting of many thousands of plants and seeds. It also contains a hint about what must be happening deep inside the living thing.

Mendel proposed an explanation: the hybrid plant forms two kinds of pollen cells and two kinds of egg cells, and each cell carries only one of the two forms. Half carry the dominant form and half the recessive, so that the hybrid sorts its inheritance into separate packets. The two forms are not blended, but only brought together, and then parted again.

A pure plant is different, for it carries the same form on both sides and so can make only one kind of cell. A plant with two copies of the round form can give only the round form to its young, however often it is crossed. The whole difference between pure plants and hybrids lies in these few simple facts about their cells.

Which pollen cell meets which egg cell is a matter of pure chance, and no cell is favoured over another. The situation is like drawing one marble from each of two bags, each bag holding equal numbers of marbles of two colours. Over many draws, the combinations will appear in fixed proportions, even though no single draw can be predicted.

Four pairings are possible: A with A, A with a, a with A, and a with a. Each is equally likely, so each should appear in about one quarter of the seeds, if the sample is large enough. Mendel's theory had thus become a prediction that could be tested against the counts.

In three of the four pairings the dominant form is present, and so it shows itself in the plant. Only in the fourth pairing, in which two recessive cells meet, does the hidden form appear, and that is why it comes back in one plant out of four. The old mystery of three to one had now become a matter of simple and elegant arithmetic.

The same four pairings also explain the ratio of one to two to one among the plants themselves. A with A gives a pure dominant plant, the two mixed pairings give hybrids, and a with a gives a pure recessive plant, which is just what his families had shown. Everything that Mendel had counted, in thousands of seeds and plants, now fitted together into one picture.

The heart of Mendel's explanation is the idea that the two forms never truly blend together. Inside the hybrid they remain separate and unchanged, and they are sorted into different cells again when the pollen and the egg cells are made. This idea, later called segregation, was quite different from the old belief that the features of the parents run together like paint.

It is worth remembering that Mendel himself never saw any of this happening with his own eyes. The microscopes of his day could not show what hidden elements were being sorted inside the cells, and so he reasoned backward from the counts to the cause. That bold step from numbers to an unseen mechanism is one of the finest examples of scientific thinking.

An explanation that merely repeats what is already known proves nothing, and Mendel understood that his idea must predict something new. He therefore looked for a test that could show it to be false, since an idea that survives such a test deserves far more trust. That is how real scientific work proceeds, and Mendel did it very well indeed.

In the first test, he crossed a hybrid with a pure plant of the hidden form. According to his theory, the hybrid would make two kinds of cells in equal numbers and the pure plant only one kind, so that half of the young should be hybrids and half pure recessive. It was a clear prediction, and the garden could prove it right or wrong.

The second test crossed a hybrid with a pure plant of the dominant form. His theory predicted that all of the young plants would show the dominant form, but that half of them would secretly be hybrids, a claim that could be checked by growing the next generation. A theory that predicts something hidden, and then invites the garden to check it, is a brave theory indeed.

To make the test sharper, Mendel followed two features at once, the shape and the colour of the seed. A hybrid for both features, his theory said, should make four kinds of cells in equal numbers, and so a cross with a plant showing both hidden forms should give four equal groups of seeds. Four groups give more ways to fail than two, so the test was a harder one.

Mendel fertilised the flowers of hybrid plants, which bore round yellow seeds, with the pollen of a plant that bore wrinkled green seeds. When the pods ripened, he opened them and sorted the seeds into four heaps according to their shape and colour. The moment of counting had arrived at last, and the theory was now truly on trial before the evidence.

The four groups came out almost equal: 31 seeds were round and yellow, 26 were round and green, 27 were wrinkled and yellow and 26 were wrinkled and green. The prediction of equal numbers had been fulfilled, within the small variations that chance allows. If the theory had been wrong, such an even pattern would have been very unlikely to appear.

Mendel then reversed the cross, so that the hybrid supplied the pollen and the wrinkled green plant supplied the egg cells. The four groups of seeds came out nearly equal in size once more, with 24, 25, 22 and 26 seeds in them. He had now examined both sides of the cross, and the evidence from the two directions was in complete agreement.

The results showed that the hybrid plant makes all four kinds of cells in equal numbers, and that it does so both for pollen and for egg cells. No other simple explanation could produce such even groups on both sides of the cross. Mendel's idea of separate and unblended forms had therefore survived a hard and searching test of its truth.

When the other parent was a pure plant with the dominant form, every one of the seeds showed the dominant form, exactly as predicted. Some of those seeds nevertheless carried the hidden form, and Mendel proved it by sowing them and watching the next generation sort itself out. The hidden form had been present all the time, unseen, like a coin in a closed hand.

Test after test had agreed with Mendel's idea, and each success made the idea harder to doubt. It was no longer a mere guess, but an explanation that had faced the garden and survived. There was still a great deal to learn, however, and the next question was what happens when more than one feature is followed at a time.

Until now, Mendel had followed one pair of features at a time, but real plants differ in many ways at once. He now asked whether two features would travel together through the generations, so that round seeds would always be yellow, or whether each would go its own way. The answer to that question would reveal how inheritance really operates, and it would prove a far-reaching one.

Mendel crossed a plant whose seeds were round and yellow with a plant whose seeds were wrinkled and green. One parent showed both dominant forms and the other showed both recessive forms, so the cross brought the two pairs together in the most direct way. Both of the parents were pure, since each of them came from a variety that had bred true for years.

All of the seeds of the first generation were round and yellow, which are the two dominant forms. This was exactly what the earlier experiments had led Mendel to expect, and it gave no hint of the surprise to come. The hybrid plants that grew from those seeds would hold the real secret of the experiment within them.

Mendel planted the hybrid seeds, let the young plants fertilise themselves, and gathered the harvest from fifteen of them. The pods held 556 seeds in all, and these he spread out on a table to sort, one by one, by their shape and colour. A small heap of peas on a table was about to tell him something of the greatest importance.

The 556 seeds fell into four quite distinct groups, which Mendel sorted and counted with the greatest care. There were 315 that were round and yellow, 101 that were wrinkled and yellow, 108 that were round and green, and 32 that were wrinkled and green. At first sight the figures look like a jumble, but they conceal a remarkably neat and regular order.

Two of the four groups were entirely new combinations, wrinkled yellow seeds and round green seeds, which neither of the original parents had possessed. The two features had therefore not travelled together, but had been shuffled like cards and dealt out in new ways. This was already a sign that the pairs of features act independently of one another.

Taken alone and considered apart from the other, each feature still gave its familiar ratio of three to one. There were 423 round seeds to 133 wrinkled ones, and 416 yellow seeds to 140 green ones, just as if the other feature had not been there at all. The two pairs of features were acting separately, without disturbing each other in the least.

The four groups came close to the ratio of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, a pattern that Mendel could have guessed from the single features. For 556 seeds, that ratio gives about 313, 104, 104 and 35, and his actual counts of 315, 101, 108 and 32 lay remarkably near. It was difficult for anyone who saw the figures side by side to call this a chance result.

The reason is simple multiplication, just as the chance of two separate events happening together is the product of the two separate chances. One feature gives three parts to one, the other gives three parts to one, and combined they make nine, three, three and one. Chance, working on each feature separately and without any knowledge of the other, had built the larger pattern.

Here was Mendel's second great finding: each pair of features is inherited independently of every other pair. The shape of the seed has no influence on its colour, and the colour has none on the shape, as if two dials were being turned quite separately. Later scientists named this principle the law of independent assortment, and it is still taught to students today.

In Mendel's letters, the hybrid for both pairs of features is written AaBb, with A and a for the shape of the seed and B and b for its colour. It forms four kinds of pollen cells and four kinds of egg cells, called AB, Ab, aB and ab, in equal numbers. Every one of the four kinds of cells is equally likely to take part in any single act of fertilisation.

Four kinds of pollen can meet four kinds of egg cells, and so there are sixteen possible pairings in all. Today they are drawn as a square of sixteen boxes, a device invented in the early twentieth century by the English scientist Reginald Punnett. Each box is equally likely, which turns a question about plants into a question about careful counting.

Counting the boxes, we find that nine of the sixteen show round yellow seeds, three show wrinkled yellow seeds, three show round green seeds and one shows wrinkled green seeds. This is exactly the ratio that Mendel had found in his garden, so the counts and the arithmetic agree. Chance, working quietly through the sixteen boxes of the square, had drawn the very pattern that he had found.

Behind the four appearances there are really nine different kinds of plants, because seeds that look alike may carry different hidden forms. The round yellow group alone includes four kinds, from the pure plant to the double hybrid. Mendel suspected this, and he knew that the way to prove it was to sow the seeds and wait.

To test the idea, Mendel planted 301 of the round yellow seeds, each in its own labelled spot, and watched every plant to the end of the summer. If his theory was right, the plants should split into four groups, in a ratio that he could calculate in advance. It was a daring experiment, because if the theory was wrong the plants would say so plainly.

The 301 plants split into four groups of very different sizes, and Mendel counted each one with care. Thirty-eight of them gave only round yellow seeds, 65 gave round yellow and round green seeds, 60 gave round yellow and wrinkled yellow seeds, and 138 gave all four kinds together. The groups were of very unequal sizes, and Mendel wanted to know whether the sizes had a meaning.

His idea predicted that the proportions should be one, two, two and four, because of the way the cells combine. Only one seed in nine is pure for both features, whereas four in nine are double hybrids that can give all four kinds of seeds. The counts of 38, 65, 60 and 138 matched the forecast closely, and the forecast had been made before the plants grew.

The wrinkled yellow seeds were tested in the same way, and of the plants that grew, 28 gave only wrinkled yellow seeds while 68 gave both wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green. That is again a ratio close to one to two, which is what the theory demanded. Each new test closed one more way in which his idea might have failed.

The round green seeds gave 35 plants that bred true and 67 that gave both round and wrinkled green seeds, once more a ratio near one to two. The 32 wrinkled green seeds carried both hidden forms, so they bred true every time, which is exactly what any pure plant must do. The theory had now been tried against all four groups and had passed them all.

Mendel summed up the result of all of these experiments in a clear and simple statement. A hybrid forms as many kinds of cells as there are possible combinations of its differing features, and each combination appears equally often. From that single sentence, the whole pattern of nine, three, three and one follows by simple calculation.

Next, Mendel crossed plants that differed in three pairs of features at once: the shape of the seed, its colour, and the colour of the seed coat. The first generation of hybrids again showed only the three dominant forms and nothing of the other three. The second generation, however, was likely to be much richer, and he prepared to count it with great care.

With three pairs of features, a hybrid plant makes eight kinds of pollen cells and eight kinds of egg cells, in equal numbers. These can meet in sixty-four ways, and the plants that result can look like eight different kinds in the ratio 27 : 9 : 9 : 9 : 3 : 3 : 3 : 1. The pattern grows more complicated as the features are added, but its logic remains exactly the same throughout.

Those eight appearances hide 27 different kinds of plants, according to what each one carries inside. Mendel's counts agreed well with the rule even when the groups became so numerous, which shows how reliable the rule was. The more complicated the cross becomes, the more convincing a successful match between theory and counts must be.

With four pairs of features, a hybrid makes sixteen kinds of cells, and the next generation can include no fewer than 81 different kinds of plants. Of these, sixteen look different from one another, since each of the four features shows either the dominant form or the recessive one. The numbers grow with astonishing speed, but they follow a rule that is perfectly clear and regular.

Mendel found a general rule that holds however many pairs of features are involved. Each new pair doubles the number of kinds of cells that a hybrid can make, and it multiplies the number of different kinds of plants by three. A short rule of this kind can describe a very large number of possibilities.

With all seven pairs of features, a hybrid would make 128 kinds of cells, and its offspring could include 2,187 different kinds of plants. To see every one of them, a gardener would need many thousands of plants, since there are 16,384 possible pairings of cells. From seven simple pairs of features, nature can build a very great variety of different living plants.

This helps to explain something that anybody can see, namely that brothers and sisters differ even when they have the same two parents. A few simple rules, applied by chance to many pairs of features, can produce an enormous number of different offspring. Variety is not a flaw in the working of inheritance, but rather one of its direct and natural results.

Mendel did not stop with a single combination of features, for he crossed plants in several different pairings and followed them for years. Each of them behaved according to the same rule, which showed that the pattern did not belong only to seed shape and seed colour. It was a general pattern, and Mendel was careful to say so in his paper with great clarity.

Because the features are shuffled, Mendel's crosses created entirely new pure varieties of pea. Peas that were round and green, or wrinkled and yellow, appeared among the descendants and then bred true, even though neither original parent had looked like that. A breeder who understood the rule could use it to design a variety on purpose.

By now Mendel had a clear and well-tested rule for his peas, and he was too good a scientist to stop there. He wondered whether other plants would follow the same pattern, and he turned to the garden bean as the next candidate. What he found in the beans was both encouraging and puzzling, and it kept him thinking for a long time.

Mendel crossed two kinds of bean, which he called Phaseolus multiflorus and Phaseolus nanus. One was a tall climbing plant with red flowers, and the other was a short bush bean with white flowers, so they differed in several clear ways. He hoped that the beans would obey the same simple rules that the peas had obeyed so faithfully.

The bean flowers gave a far more complicated result than the peas had done. In the second generation the colours ranged through many shades, from deep purple-red to white, and not just two clear forms. Mendel could see that something more elaborate and more subtle was happening in the beans than in the peas.

Mendel suggested a clever answer: that the flower colour of the bean was built from several separate pairs of features working together, each pair following the same rule as in the peas. If that were so, then the many shades would be simple combinations of the same few forms. He admitted that the experiments were not yet finished, and that they needed much more time.

Later scientists showed that Mendel had been right to suspect a team of factors. Many features, such as the height of a person or the colour of skin, depend on many genes working together, each adding a small effect. The simple ratios of the pea are only the clearest case of a very general pattern.

Not all plants follow the pea pattern of complete dominance, in which one form simply hides the other. When a red marvel of Peru is crossed with a white one, the young plants bear pink flowers, which seems at first like the old blending idea. Yet when those pink plants are bred together, the red and white forms come back unchanged, in the same pattern of one to two to one.

Earlier breeders had noticed that hybrids tend to go back, in later generations, to the forms of their original parents. Mendel's rule explains the puzzle, since the pure parental forms are being made again in every generation, in the proportions that his families had shown. What had looked like a strange habit of nature turned out to be a matter of arithmetic.

In his closing remarks, Mendel asked what hybrids might reveal about the origin of new forms of life, a question that was much discussed in the years after Darwin's book. He was careful, however, to claim no more than his own experiments had shown, and he did not let his imagination run ahead of the counts. That caution is a large part of what makes the paper so trustworthy, even to readers of a later age.

One reason for Mendel's success was that he treated living things with mathematics, which was very unusual in the biology of his time. His training in physics and mathematics at Vienna helped him to see patterns in counts that a naturalist trained only in description might never have noticed. The monastery garden had become a kind of laboratory of numbers as well as a laboratory of living plants.

Mendel's method can be put into a few plain words, and it is worth remembering them one by one. He chose features that were clear, crossed his plants under strict control, followed every generation separately, and counted every plant. Simple though it sounds, almost nobody before him had combined all four steps in a single experiment.

Mendel wrote up eight years of work as a long and careful paper, in plain language and with its figures set out in tables that anyone could check. He did not boast about his results, and he reported only what he had seen in the garden. Its quiet confidence is the mark of a scientist who knows his figures and trusts them completely.

Mendel was a member of the Natural History Society of Brünn, a club that had been founded a few years earlier for people who loved to study nature. Its members were teachers, doctors and other citizens of the town who met to hear talks and to discuss each other's work. It was an ordinary audience, not a famous one, and it did not know what it was about to hear.

On 8 February 1865, Mendel stood before the Society and read the first part of his paper aloud. He described his peas, his seven pairs of features and the strange return of the hidden forms in the second generation. The listeners had never heard a talk quite like it, and they had no way of knowing how important it was.

The members listened politely, but they do not seem to have grasped the importance of what they had heard. Accounts of the evening suggest that there was little discussion, and no one seems to have asked the questions that a modern scientist would ask at once. The talk was about peas, and peas were not thought to be a great subject.

A month later, on 8 March, Mendel returned to give the second part, in which he explained his theory and showed how the letters combined. Here the talk became harder for listeners who had come to hear about gardening, since it was full of mathematics. He had given them a rule for inheritance, and they had received it as a curiosity.

The paper was printed in 1866 in the journal of the Society, under a title that means Experiments on Plant Hybrids. It filled more than forty pages, and every table and every figure was there for anyone to check. A great discovery had been published in a small journal, in a provincial town, in a language that few foreign scientists read for pleasure.

The Society's journal was sent in the post to libraries and scientific societies in many countries, so the paper did reach other readers. Mendel also had a few dozen separate copies of his own paper printed, and he sent them to scientists whose opinion he valued. He did what an author can do, and then he waited for a reply.

For more than thirty years the paper was hardly noticed, and the few scientists who mentioned it saw it as one more study of hybrids rather than a discovery of a law. The reasons are still discussed: it was published in a small journal, it was written in a style that was quite new, and its ideas were ahead of what most biologists were ready to think. A great idea can sometimes wait a very long time before it finds an audience that is ready for it.

At the end of 1866 Mendel wrote to Carl Nägeli, a leading botanist in Munich, and sent him a copy of the paper. He hoped for an expert opinion from a man whose judgement on plants counted for a great deal. It was a modest and respectful letter, written by a monk in a provincial town to a famous professor.

Nägeli replied politely, but he was not convinced that the peas showed a general law, and he thought the results needed testing on other plants. He advised Mendel to try the hawkweed, a plant that Nägeli himself was studying, and Mendel agreed. It was a well-meant suggestion from an honest critic, and as it turned out, it was also an unlucky one.

The hawkweed did not follow the rules of the peas, and Mendel, who reported his results in a second paper in 1869, could not tell why. The reason was only found long after his death: many hawkweeds can make seeds without fertilisation, so their young are copies of the parent. His peas had given him a clear law, but the hawkweed gave him only questions.

His main pea experiments had run from about 1856 to 1863, and in later years Mendel turned to other interests. He kept bees and tried to cross different kinds, he studied the weather, and he kept careful records of temperature and rain. His curiosity never grew tired, even though the great discovery was already behind him.

In 1870 a violent whirlwind crossed the town of Brünn, and Mendel, who was already a keen observer of the weather, studied the damage with care. He wrote a report on the path that the storm had followed and on the signs that it had left behind. The same patient eye that had counted so many thousands of peas could also describe a violent storm.

In 1868 the monks of the monastery elected Mendel as their new abbot, a post of honour that also carried a great weight of responsibility. He was now in charge of the whole community and its property, which included lands, buildings and a heavy burden of accounts. The scientist had now become a manager of men and money, and the garden began slowly to recede.

As abbot, Mendel had far less time for experiments, and little by little he gave up his plant crosses. His duties filled the days with meetings, letters and accounts, and the garden was left more and more to others. He had finished the work that he had set out to do, and he had no way of knowing how it would be valued.

In 1874 the government passed a law that laid a new and heavy tax on monasteries, and Mendel thought it unjust. He refused to pay, and the quarrel dragged on for years, bringing him much worry and some bitterness. It is a reminder that the quiet monk in the garden was also a man of firm will.

People who knew Mendel remembered him as a kind and generous man who loved his garden and his bees. He gave money to the poor and helped students who lacked the means to study, as his sister Theresia had once helped him. Whatever else he had to do, he did not forget the people who needed him.

In his last years Mendel's health declined, and he died in Brünn in January 1884, at the age of 61. The cause was a disease of the kidneys, and the funeral was attended by many people who remembered him as a good abbot. Few of them, if any, thought of him as a scientist whose name would one day be known in every school.

According to the accounts that survive, many of Mendel's private papers were burned soon after his death, so that historians know less about his work than they would wish. The printed paper, however, had been saved in libraries, where it sat on the shelves in many different cities. Fortunately for science, a printed page that has been sent out into the world can be very hard to destroy.

People who knew Mendel later reported that, near the end of his life, the old abbot had said, “My time will come.” We cannot be certain of the exact words, but whether or not he said them, they proved to be prophetic. That time did arrive, but only sixteen years after his death, when three scientists rediscovered his work.

During those same years, Charles Darwin had argued that living things change over time, but he had no sound explanation of how features are passed from parents to offspring. His own guesses, made in the old language of blending, did not fit the facts well. The missing piece was lying in a monastery's printed journal, and nobody knew where to look for it.

In the spring of 1900, three scientists in three different countries reported the same pattern in their own experiments with plants. They had worked separately and had no plan to publish together, yet their results agreed with each other, and each showed ratios close to three to one. It was one of the great coincidences in the history of science, and historians have never tired of discussing it.

Hugo de Vries, a Dutch botanist, had crossed many kinds of plants, and he found the three-to-one ratio in several of them. In March 1900 he was the first of the three to publish his results, and in a later paper he gave Mendel the credit for the earlier discovery. The debt to the old monk was acknowledged, though not at first very loudly.

Carl Correns, in Germany, had worked with peas and with maize, and he reached the same ratios by his own road. Only after he had worked out the pattern did he find Mendel's old paper in the literature, and he was astonished to see how complete it already was. He wrote up his own results under the title Mendel's Rule, so that the honour went to the right man.

Erich von Tschermak, in Austria, had also been crossing peas, and he soon published results that pointed the same way. Historians still disagree about how fully he understood their meaning at the time, and some give most of the credit to the other two. Whatever the truth may be, the pea garden had suddenly become a very crowded place indeed.

All three scientists accepted that Mendel had been first, and word of the forgotten paper spread quickly through the scientific world. Libraries searched their shelves for the journal, and people who had never heard of Brünn were soon reading about the abbot's peas. Thirty-four years after it had first been printed, the paper was at last being heard by the world.

In England, William Bateson became Mendel's most vigorous champion, arguing for the new ideas in lectures, books and heated debates. In 1901 he had the old paper translated into English, so that readers who knew no German could study it for themselves. Without his energy and his stubborn enthusiasm, the rediscovery might have moved much more slowly than it did.

A few years later, Bateson suggested a name for the new study of inheritance, and the name was genetics. It comes from a Greek word that is linked with origin and birth, and it caught on at once. Mendel's quiet pea garden had given birth to a whole new field of science, and now it had a proper name.

Scientists soon tested Mendel's rules on many other living things, including mice, chickens, maize and fruit flies. In case after case the main pattern held true, and so the rules were seen not as a curiosity of peas but as a feature of life itself. The patient work of the old abbot was becoming the secure foundation of a whole new science.

Doctors soon found that some inherited human conditions also seem to follow Mendel's rules in families. In 1902 the English physician Archibald Garrod showed that a rare inherited condition appeared in families in just the pattern that a recessive form would produce, and that it affected the way the body handles certain chemicals. Heredity in human beings was not a mystery without rules after all, and the same patterns applied.

At first, some scientists refused to accept Mendel's rules, especially those who studied features such as height, which vary smoothly and do not fall into two clear groups. The argument between the two sides of the dispute was long and at times quite bitter. It was settled only when scientists showed that many small Mendelian factors, working together, can produce exactly such smooth variation.

Since about 1880, scientists using the microscope had seen small thread-like bodies inside dividing cells, and they called these chromosomes, a name that means coloured bodies. Nobody knew what the chromosomes were for, only that they were carefully shared out when a cell divided into two. The link with Mendel's hidden factors, which nobody had yet connected with them, was still waiting to be made.

In 1902 and 1903, Walter Sutton in America and Theodor Boveri in Germany noticed that chromosomes behave exactly as Mendel's hidden factors were supposed to behave. They come in pairs, one from each parent, and the pairs are separated into different cells when pollen and egg cells are made. The unseen cause of Mendel's ratios might therefore be something that could actually be seen under a microscope.

In 1909 the Danish scientist Wilhelm Johannsen gave the hidden factors a short and useful name, and he called them genes. Mendel never heard the word, and he could not have imagined how important it would become. Yet every time we use it, we are talking about the thing that he reasoned out from his peas.

In 1910, Thomas Hunt Morgan, working in New York, spotted a single fruit fly with white eyes among thousands with red eyes. By following its descendants through many generations, he and his students showed that a particular gene sits on a particular chromosome. The fruit fly, small and cheap and quick to breed, became the pea of the twentieth century.

Morgan's group found that genes lying close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, a pattern that is called linkage. It is an exception to Mendel's rule of independent assortment, although a gentle one, since genes that lie far apart on a chromosome still sort almost independently. The rules, in other words, needed some adjusting, but they certainly did not need to be replaced.

Peas have seven pairs of chromosomes, and Mendel studied seven features, which has led some people to say that he was very lucky. The genes for his features lie either on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one, and so they sorted independently, just as his rule says. His careful choice of clear features, together with a measure of good fortune, made the pattern easy to see.

For many years after Mendel's discovery nobody knew with certainty what genes were really made of. In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix structure of DNA, building on the X-ray pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin and on the work of other scientists. The shape showed at once how a molecule could carry a message and be copied when a cell divides.

A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries instructions for building some part of a living thing. The two forms that Mendel followed in each pair of features are simply two versions of the same instruction, and the dominant version is the one that shows when both are present. His hidden factors had finally been given a physical home inside the living cell, written in a chemical code.

In 1990, more than a century after Mendel's paper, scientists found the very gene that makes some of his peas wrinkled. A change in that gene alters how the seed stores starch and sugar, and as the seed dries it shrinks into folds. The hidden factor of the monk's notebook had become a piece of text that could be read.

In 1936 the statistician Ronald Fisher pointed out that some of Mendel's counts were closer to the expected ratios than chance usually allows. Historians have offered several explanations, such as unconscious bias in sorting doubtful seeds, and the debate continues to this day. What nobody disputes is that experiments repeated by many other scientists have confirmed Mendel's rules.

Today, pupils all over the world grow peas, or use counters and coins as models, and count the results as Mendel did. They are often surprised when their own numbers come close to the famous three to one, because a rule that was found in a monastery garden turns up on a classroom desk. Every student who sees it for themselves repeats a small part of the old discovery.

Mendel's two main findings are now called the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment. The first says that the two forms of a feature are separated again when the sex cells are made, and the second says that different pairs of features are sorted independently, though with the exceptions that Morgan found. Together they form the firm base on which the rest of the science of genetics now stands.

Farmers and breeders now use Mendel's ideas every day to improve crops and animals, choosing their parents on purpose and keeping the young that show the right features. A variety of wheat that resists disease or a bean that gives a bigger harvest may owe a great deal to rules first found in a monastery. What had once been guesswork and tradition became a careful craft that could be taught and learned.

Doctors and genetic counsellors use the same kind of reasoning to explain how some conditions run in families, and to describe what the chances may be for a future child. Real life is usually more complicated than peas, because many features depend on several genes and on the surroundings as well. Even so, the first step in understanding such cases is the simple pattern that Mendel found.

Today, visitors to Brno can see the old Augustinian monastery where Mendel lived, which now houses a museum about his life and work. The museum tells the story of the monk, his peas and the science that grew from them. In 2022 many countries marked the two hundredth anniversary of his birth, and the quiet abbot became famous once again.

Mendel's paper is also a lesson in honesty and modesty for anybody who wishes to do real science. He reported what he had seen, he said openly where he was unsure, and he left the larger questions for others to take up. That is much of the reason why the paper can still be read with trust today.

In the same way, every one of us carries a mixture of forms from both parents, handed down in separate units and shuffled afresh by chance. That is why we resemble our families and yet are never exact copies of them, not even brothers and sisters, apart from identical twins. The rules of the pea garden are, in the end, the rules of our own lives and of our own families.

In 2003 scientists announced that they had read nearly all of the human genome, a code about three billion letters long. The great project had its roots in the questions that a monk had asked about peas, and in the idea that inheritance comes in separate units that can be counted. Every page of that code is written in a language that Mendel could only guess at.

Over the years, scientists have found the genes behind several of Mendel's seven features, and they have found that his careful descriptions were accurate. In 2019 the complete genome of the pea was published, so the plant that opened the subject has now been read from end to end. The monk's garden and the modern laboratory are tied together by one small green seed.

Mendel's garden was small and his equipment was simple, no more than a brush, some bags, a notebook and a great deal of patience. With those modest means he asked a clear question, counted the answer and found a law that helps us to understand every living thing, from the pea plant to ourselves. The lesson of his paper is that careful, honest experiments, repeated often enough, can reveal the hidden order beneath ordinary appearances.
